headline: Anthropic revealed in its September 2026 report on detecting and combating AI misuse that a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen, in Houthi-controlled territory, was running three weapons development programs with the assistance of Claude and Claude Code. The cell was developing a guided rocket using a commodity phone-class flight computer with final-phase homing guidance; a multistage ballistic missile with a stated range goal of more than 2,000 km; and a multi-variant missile family referred to as the “R2000” set, including a variant with a Hypersonic Glide Vehicle (HGV). Anthropic said the actors used Claude Code in place of human software engineers to develop the guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) software used to steer and stabilize the vehicles. The work included integrating an open-source autopilot with a phone-class flight computer, writing control and position-estimation software, tuning control settings, running a firmware build pipeline, and conducting flight simulations. The actors also managed several Claude instances simultaneously, assigning each one a different role in a manner similar to a small engineering team. One instance was tasked with writing code, another with research, and a third with reviewing the code produced by the first. Anthropic said its safeguards blocked many of the actors’ requests, but not all of them. According to the report, the actors used various tactics to evade the safeguards, including concealing their goals and the products the software was intended for. They also split their work across multiple sessions so that no single session revealed the full scope of the project. Anthropic said it has no evidence that the actors successfully fielded an operational weapon. However, the company confirmed that they did test-fire a guided rocket. The field test appears to have failed, with the actors returning to Claude within hours to determine why it had failed. Anthropic said it banned the accounts associated with the activity and shared threat information with public- and private-sector partners to help mitigate the risks posed by the actors. However, the report also noted that the actors had already developed an offline simulation toolkit that did not rely on Claude or other engineering computing environments such as MATLAB.

headline: The Wall Street Journal reports that Iran has resumed low rate ballistic missile production, using stockpiled components and underground facilities despite extensive U.S. and Israeli strikes on its missile infrastructure. U.S. and regional officials say Iran is primarily assembling missiles from existing warheads, airframes and guidance systems, with activity identified at multiple underground sites including the Khojir complex. Production remains below prewar levels because strikes damaged key industrial facilities and the blockade has complicated access to components and solid fuel materials. One U.S. official assessed Iran could assemble at least a few hundred missiles from supplies currently on hand. The renewed production is occurring alongside evidence that Iran is rebuilding damaged missile infrastructure, including reopening tunnel entrances and repairing access roads. Iran has continued launching ballistic missiles against U.S. positions in the region, including a heavy salvo against Muwaffaq al Salti Air Base damaging several F-15s and taking the wing off of an A-10. Source: https://www.wsj.com/world/middle-east/iran-ballistic-missile-production-5538af12?st

headline: Reuters reports that Britain, Norway and the United States disrupted a Russian undersea warfare exercise near Svalbard this spring, after detecting Russian vessels associated with Russia’s Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research (GUGI) using deep sea submersibles to simulate deployment of a new weapon intended to disable subsea cables. The exercise did not damage any cables, but Western officials told Reuters it focused on practicing how the technology could be used during a conflict with NATO. The operation occurred near two 1,400-km fiber-optic cables connecting Svalbard to mainland Norway, which carry satellite data from SvalSat, the world’s largest satellite ground station. The incident comes amid growing NATO concerns over Russian activity around critical undersea infrastructure. Reuters reports that ships have increasingly been observed slowly passing over or near cables and pipelines, potentially mapping them for future use, while NATO and European countries have expanded monitoring through initiatives including Baltic Sentry and Nordic Warden. The three Western countries confronted the Russian vessels at sea, while British and Norwegian officials separately presented Moscow with evidence that they were aware of the technology and its use. Norway’s defense minister said the operation was intended to make clear that attempts to covertly target critical infrastructure would be detected and face consequences. Russia has not commented on the specific incident and routinely denies conducting sabotage operations against NATO countries. Source: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/nato-allies-foil-russian-subsea-cable-sabotage-plot-2026-09-10
